title: Bonanza Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Bonanza wells have a 160-foot median depth, 8 gpm median yield, and typical finished-well costs of $14,000-$24,000.
h1: Bonanza, Colorado Well Depths, Yields and Costs
intro_html:
Well records within 5 miles of Bonanza show a groundwater area with moderate typical depths but wide variability. The median permitted well is 160 feet deep, while the middle half runs from 88 to 255 feet. Most reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, but records are incomplete: 110 wells appear in the Colorado Division of Water Resources permit data, 76 are recorded as constructed, and 37 report a pump yield.

Bonanza is in Saguache County, near Saguache, Poncha Springs, Maysville, Salida, Howard and Coaldale. Use these figures to screen a property, not to guarantee its result. A driller still needs to evaluate the exact lot, access, geology, casing and grouting requirements, and the intended household or stock use.

sections.heading: Bonanza well depths range from shallow to very deep
sections.html:
Bonanza’s median well depth is 160 feet, and the middle half of recorded depths falls between 88 and 255 feet. The depth mix shows why a single bid can be misleading: 30% are under 100 feet, 46% are between 100 and 300 feet, 20% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 4% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record reaches 1,780 feet.

The permits mainly identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 103 wells in that category. Fractured rock can change quickly across short distances, so nearby well depths are useful evidence but not a promise. For a Bonanza drilling estimate, ask for a written allowance that explains how the price changes if the hole goes beyond the expected depth, and confirm casing and grout are included.

sections.heading: Reported Bonanza yields are generally usable, but records are limited
sections.html:
The median reported pump yield near Bonanza is 8.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5.0 and 13.0 gallons per minute. Seventy percent of reported wells fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, 14% report more than 15 gallons per minute, and 16% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute.

That is a favorable local pattern, but only 37 wells report a pump yield. Yield is not the same as storage in the well or guaranteed household flow. A buyer should request the well construction report, pump information and any available pumping test. A home with storage tanks may handle variable production better than a system designed around continuous high demand.

sections.heading: Water levels are shallow in the few Bonanza records available
sections.html:
Only 4 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is small. Those records show a median depth to water of 2 feet, with the middle half from 1 to 24 feet. This suggests shallow measured water levels in the reported wells, but it does not establish a reliable water-table elevation for every lot.

The permit history does not provide enough water-level observations by decade to demonstrate a falling or rising trend. Do not treat the shallow median as proof that drilling will be easy or that pumping capacity is high. Static water level, seasonal conditions, well depth and actual production are separate questions. Ask for recent measurements and compare neighboring construction reports where available.

sections.heading: Bonanza drilling history reaches back to the 1970s
sections.html:
Permit activity is concentrated in the 2000s, when 38 permits were issued. The records show 5 permits in the 1970s, 14 in the 1980s, 22 in the 1990s, 38 in the 2000s, 14 in the 2010s and 5 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025, so the area still has recent drilling information.

American Drilling Service, associated in the records with Dewberry, Bradford W., appears most often with 37 wells. Mccoy Drilling Inc, associated with Dennison, Lynn A., appears with 12, and Moody Drilling, associated with Moody, Michael C., with 5. These records show who has worked nearby, not who is available or recommended today. Verify licensing, insurance, references and the proposed scope before hiring.

sections.heading: A Bonanza well budget starts around the median depth
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground described in the local cost model, drilling commonly runs about $50-$75 per foot. At Bonanza’s 160-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $8,000-$12,000. A finished system, including pump, tank, trenching and electrical, is modeled at about $14,000-$24,000.

That finished-well range is a planning figure, not a fixed quote. Access, difficult ground, additional casing, power requirements, trench length and the final pump setup can change the total. Ask whether the proposal covers permitting, mobilization, casing, grout, development, pump installation, pressure equipment, electrical work and testing. Also ask for the cost of a dry hole or an unsuccessful completion before drilling starts.

sections.heading: Mine history, septic layout and water rights deserve a close check
sections.html:
Within about 10 miles of Bonanza, the mapped environmental data includes 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 613 historic mine features and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These counts do not prove contamination at a particular parcel. They do justify checking the property history, nearby mine workings, water testing records and applicable environmental databases before closing.

Low yield and dry holes remain practical risks in fractured-bedrock settings, even with a solid nearby median. Have the well location, septic system, reserve area, driveway and building footprint reviewed together. Colorado DWR permits control the authorized use; many household wells are exempt wells, and the 35 gpm exempt-well pumping limit still matters. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required. Confirm the permit’s use, and test existing water before relying on it.

sections.heading: What to do before buying or building near Bonanza
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not the area average. Pull neighboring DWR well records and compare depths, reported yields, aquifer descriptions and construction details. The local records show 88% domestic or household use, 25% stock use, 2% irrigation and 5% monitoring, so confirm that the existing permit actually supports the use you need.

Before making an offer, make the contract contingent on reviewing the well permit, construction report, water quality and septic feasibility. If the lot is vacant, have a driller evaluate rig access and a civil or septic professional reserve suitable space before you choose the building site. For a new home, budget the complete system rather than drilling alone, and keep a contingency for deeper drilling, low production or an alternate water plan.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Bonanza, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within 5 miles of Bonanza is 160 feet. The middle half runs from 88 to 255 feet, but the range is wide: 30% are under 100 feet, while 4% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record is 1,780 feet, so neighboring wells should guide expectations without being treated as a guarantee.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Bonanza?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50-$75 per foot. At Bonanza’s 160-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $8,000-$12,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $14,000-$24,000. Access, casing, ground conditions, electrical work and final equipment can move the quote.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Bonanza?
faq.a: The median reported yield near Bonanza is 8.0 gallons per minute. The middle half of reported yields is 5.0-13.0 gallons per minute, and 70% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Only 37 wells report a yield, so request the construction report and pumping information for the specific property.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Bonanza, Colorado?
faq.a: The area has 2 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 613 historic mine features and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those records do not establish contamination on a parcel, but they support testing before use. Test existing wells and review nearby mine and environmental history rather than assuming water is safe.

faq.q: Are Bonanza wells good for a new home?
faq.a: Reported production is generally useful, with a median of 8.0 gallons per minute and no reported well under 1 gallon per minute. Still, only 37 wells report yield, and fractured-bedrock results can vary sharply. Confirm the permit allows household use, verify water quality, and coordinate the well, septic area, driveway and building site before buying or building.
